<reason>A genuinely top-tier debate decided by execution and rebuttal precision. B had the single most powerful substantive idea — grievances must be formed, and invisible patterns never trigger CON's litigation remedy — and pressed it memorably from R1 through closing. But A built the more consistent architecture (standard vs. machinery; triggered vs. standing disclosure), answered both pressure questions directly with labels, and in Rebuttal 2 landed the debate's sharpest counter-turn, mapped B's concessions into a "the motion has collapsed" narrative, and weighed scalpel-vs-warehouse cleanly. A's closing then resolved the choice into one crisp decision rule. B's pattern-detection route survived only partially against A's staleness/treadmill critique of standing filings, and B was clipped twice — an execution cost the format rules say to count. B's rhetoric was the more quotable, but A made the close contest slightly easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 2 (A1 answer): under B's own asymmetric design, workers receive only "materiality," never the threshold — the specification goes to the regulator — so B's signature jammed-scanner worker is fired at an unseen threshold in B's world too, and only grievance-triggered discovery actually reaches the scanner records. This neutralized B's most emotive example while preserving A's alternative, and B never squarely recovered that individual-case point.</best_rebuttal>
